raw_findings.body: `z.string().toString()` evaluates to "[object Object]" at object-literal construction, so both computed entries collide into a single bogus key and the schema effectively only declares `access_token`. Zod strips undeclared keys by default, so expiry fields (expiry_date/expires_in), refresh_token, scope, etc. are silently dropped from `data`; the intended 'any numeric expiry' validation never happens and downstream code stores credentials with missing expiry, causing NaN/undefined expiry dates.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Token responses in sync mode are stripped down to access_token only, persisting incomplete credentials and defeating the validation the schema was meant to perform.
raw_findings.impact: `z.string().toString()` evaluates to "[object Object]" at object-literal construction, so both computed entries collide into a single bogus key and the schema effectively only declares `access_token`. Zod strips undeclared keys by default, so expiry fields (expiry_date/expires_in), refresh_token, scope, etc. are silently dropped from `data`; the intended 'any numeric expiry' validation never happens and downstream code stores credentials with missing expiry, causing NaN/undefined expiry dates.
raw_findings.root_cause: Computed object-literal keys evaluate the Zod instance's toString() at construction time; they do not create pattern-based schema keys.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Define the schema explicitly (e.g. `z.object({ access_token: z.string() }).passthrough()` plus an explicit refinement for an expiry field) instead of computed keys derived from Zod instances.
raw_findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed keys from Zod instances, producing a meaningless '[object Object]' property and stripping all token fields
raw_findings.trigger: Credential sharing enabled with CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT set; any token refresh parsed via the minimum schema.

finding.body: `z.string().toString()` evaluates to "[object Object]" at object-literal construction, so both computed entries collide into a single bogus key and the schema effectively only declares `access_token`. validated_findings.failure_mode: Wasted token-endpoint round trip on every operation and possible use of an expired access token despite a fresh one being available.
validated_findings.impact: Each calendar operation issues a refresh-token grant to Salesforce (extra latency, API/rate-limit consumption), yet the jsforce Connection below is still constructed with the stale `credentialKey.access_token` rather than `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`, so the newly fetched token is only written to the DB and never used in-session.

validated_findings.suggested_fix: Only refresh when the stored token is expired, and pass the refreshed access_token (and instance_url) into the jsforce Connection.
validated_findings.title: Salesforce token refresh runs unconditionally on every client construction and the refreshed token is never used by the returned connection

validated_findings.verifier_reason: Patch shows refresh runs unconditionally in getClient (lines R75-R99) with no expiry check, and the jsforce Connection at R105-R107 uses `credentialKey.access_token` (the old token) not the refreshed `accessTokenParsed.data.access_token`. validated_findings.impact: In sync mode refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw `fetch` Response, which has no `.data` property (unlike the gaxios response used in the fallback branch). `res?.data` is undefined, `token.access_token` throws a TypeError which is swallowed by the catch block, so the token is never refreshed and Google Calendar silently keeps using an expired token — the sync feature is non-functional for Google.
validated_findings.root_cause: refreshOAuthTokens returns heterogeneous types (fetch Response vs. gaxios response) and the caller only handles the gaxios shape.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Normalize the sync response (e.g. `await response.json()`) inside refreshOAuthTokens or in this caller before reading token fields.

validated_findings.body: String `!==` comparison of the shared webhook secret is not constant-time, theoretically enabling timing side-channel attacks against an endpoint that can write arbitrary third-party credentials into any user's account.
validated_findings.failure_mode: Timing-based secret disclosure risk on a credential-writing endpoint.
validated_findings.impact: String `!==` comparison of the shared webhook secret is not constant-time, theoretically enabling timing side-channel attacks against an endpoint that can write arbitrary third-party credentials into any user's account.
validated_findings.root_cause: Secret authenticated via ordinary string comparison.
validated_findings.suggested_fix: Compare with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers (rejecting non-string/array header values first).
validated_findings.title: Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time `!==`
validated_findings.trigger: An attacker probing the endpoint with candidate secrets and measuring response timing.
validated_findings.verifier_reason: Timing side-channel on string comparison is a theoretical concern requiring precise timing measurements. The endpoint is already protected by a shared secret and feature flag. Low practical exploitability for this context.
